content: Contraception, also known as birth control, is primarily utilized to prevent unintended pregnancies through various methods, including devices, sexual practices, chemicals, medications, or surgical procedures. Additionally, contraceptive methods may serve other purposes, such as preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or managing medical conditions like acne, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), endometriosis, amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, premenstrual syndrome (PMS), primary ovarian insufficiency (POI), and heavy menstrual bleeding. When selecting the most suitable contraceptive method for individuals or couples, healthcare providers must consider factors such as safety, effectiveness, accessibility, affordability, and acceptability. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has established guidelines and categories to assess the safety of various contraceptive methods. Female Contraceptive Options 1. Long-Acting Reversible Contraception (LARC): These methods are over 99% effective, provide long-term contraception, and allow for a rapid return to fertility upon discontinuation. Intrauterine Devices (IUDs): Copper IUD: Effective for up to 10 years. It is suitable for individuals with light menstrual periods or those seeking long-term contraception without hormones. Progestin-Releasing IUD: Effective for up to 5 years. It is recommended for individuals with heavy menstrual bleeding or dysmenorrhea. Subdermal Implant: This method is over 99% effective and provides contraception for up to 3 years. 2. Injectable Contraception: Depot-Medroxyprogesterone Acetate (DMPA): This intramuscular injection is 94% effective and is administered every three months. 3. Combined Hormonal Contraceptives (CHCs): Oral Contraceptive Pills (OCPs): These estrogen/progestin combination pills are 91% effective. Contraceptive Patch: This method is also 91% effective. Vaginal Ring: Another CHC option with 91% effectiveness. 4. Barrier and Chemical Methods: Female Condom, Diaphragm, Cervical Cap, Sponge: These methods vary in effectiveness and are often used in combination with spermicides. Spermicide: When used alone, it has a high failure rate (80%) and may increase the risk of genital epithelial damage and STI acquisition. 5. Traditional/Natural Contraception: Fertility Awareness Methods, Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM), Abstinence, Withdrawal, Rhythm Method: These methods rely on natural cycles or behaviors and vary in effectiveness. 6. Surgical Options: Tubal Ligation (Tubectomy): A permanent sterilization method. 7. Emergency Contraception: Copper IUD: Can be used as emergency contraception. Emergency Contraceptive Pills (ECPs): These are used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse. Male Contraceptive Options 1. Barrier Contraception: Condoms: These are 80% effective and are the only contraceptive method that also protects against STIs. 2. Male Sterilization: Vasectomy: A permanent surgical method of contraception. 3. Coitus Interruptus (Withdrawal): This method is 75% effective. 4. Hormonal Contraception (Under Research and Development): Testosterone-Based Methods: Short-acting intramuscular testosterone enanthate. Long-acting intramuscular testosterone undecanoate. Combination Hormonal Regimens: Testosterone combined with progestin or gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonists. Transdermal Regimens: Testosterone combined with Nestorone in gel formulations. Oral Formulations: Commonly referred to as the male pill. Indications for Contraceptive Use 1. Contraceptive Use: Prevention of unintended pregnancies. 2. Non-Contraceptive Use: Management of medical conditions such as: Acne. Amenorrhea. Dysmenorrhea. Endometriosis. Heavy menstrual bleeding. Premenstrual syndrome (PMS). Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI). Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS): OCPs are often used for menstrual regulation. Contraindications 1. Combined Hormonal Contraceptives (CHCs): Absolute contraindications include: Pregnancy. Less than six weeks postpartum. Smoking in individuals aged 35 or older who smoke 15 or more cigarettes per day. Severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 mmHg or diastolic ≥100 mmHg). Current or past history of venous thromboembolism (VTE). History of thromboembolic events or stroke. Thrombophilia (e.g., factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome). Ischemic heart disease. History of cerebrovascular accidents. Complicated valvular heart disease. Migraine with aura or focal neurological symptoms. Active breast cancer or history of estrogen-dependent tumors. Diabetes with complications (e.g., retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy). Severe liver disease or liver tumors. Hypertriglyceridemia. Relative contraindications include: Age ≥35 and smoking fewer than 15 cigarettes per day. Migraine without aura in individuals over 35 years of age. Gallbladder disease. Mild liver disease. History of cholestasis related to combined OCP use. Use of medications that interfere with OCPs (e.g., lamotrigine, rifampin). Family history of thrombophilia with thromboembolism. 2. Intrauterine Devices (IUDs): Contraindications include: Uterine anomalies or severe distortion. Active pelvic infection. Wilson’s disease. Complicated organ transplant failure. 3. Subdermal Implants: Contraindicated in individuals with progesterone receptor-positive breast cancer. Emergency Contraception Emergency contraception options include the copper IUD and emergency contraceptive pills. Side Effects Side effects vary depending on the contraceptive method and may include hormonal, physical, or systemic effects. U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC), 2016 The CDC provides guidelines to assess the safety of contraceptive methods based on individual characteristics, including safety, effectiveness, availability, and acceptability. Dos and Don’ts 1. Dos: Increase levothyroxine doses in hypothyroid patients starting OCPs, as estrogen increases thyroxine-binding globulin levels. Adjust warfarin doses in patients using OCPs. Use two forms of contraception and conduct monthly pregnancy tests for women on isotretinoin for acne. Recommend non-oral contraceptives (e.g., IUDs, implants) for one year post-bariatric surgery to stabilize nutritional status. Consider IUDs for nulliparous women without contraindications. 2. Don’ts: Avoid prescribing CHCs to individuals aged 35 or older who smoke 15 or more cigarettes daily. Do not prescribe CHCs to patients with a history of migraines with aura or focal neurological symptoms.
